paper_summary: Singh, Kumar, Sachan and Sharma (IJERMCE 9(7), 2022) present a short student-level study titled 'Synthesis and Characterization of Syntactic foam'. After a general review of syntactic-foam types (two- vs three-phase, MMC/PMC/CMC), the actual experiment takes a commercially porous polypropylene foam as the matrix, submerges it in a semi-fluid Plaster of Paris paste so the existing pores fill up, dries it and bakes it for 1.5 h at 220 C, then compression-tests it on a UTM against a red brick reference. The reported outcome is a 35.35% density reduction (1239.90 kg/m3 vs 1922 kg/m3 for red brick) and a ~63% drop in breaking stress; the authors recommend the material only where strength is not required.
extraction_notes:
OFF-TOPIC / EXCLUDED under rule 6: this is not a hollow-particle composite. No microballoons, cenospheres or hollow spheres of any kind are added to a matrix. The authors instead take an already-cellular polypropylene foam ('microballoons are already present in it') and infiltrate its open pores with a Plaster of Paris paste - i.e. a filled cellular/open-cell foam, which is the inverse of syntactic-foam architecture (in a syntactic foam the hollow phase is a discrete particle dispersed in a dense matrix; here the solid phase is poured into the cells and the hollow phase ceases to be hollow). is_syntactic_foam_paper is therefore set false and records is empty. Only the paper's title and framing are about syntactic foams; the hollow-particle systems it cites (epoxy/hollow glass microspheres, fly-ash cenosphere/polyurethane) appear in the two-line literature review with no numerical data at all.

For a human reviewer who may wish to override this call, the numbers that exist are recorded here rather than as records, and they are unusable as they stand. Table (b) 'Syntactic foam': specimen 45.00 mm wide x 40 mm thick, cross-section 2700.0 mm2 (45 x 40 = 1800, not 2700 - the geometry is already inconsistent), peak load 5.130, compressive strength 0.194 kg/mm2, elongation at break 6.99 mm, breaking load 39.49 kN, breaking stress 0.523 kN/mm2. The last three of those are byte-identical to the red-brick row in Table (a) (6.99 / 39.49 / 0.523), so Table (b) is a copy-paste of the reference specimen's results. Table (c) then contradicts Table (b), giving the foam a breaking stress of 0.192 kg/mm2 and a yield stress of 0.165 kN/mm2 - and the two tables also swap the units between kg/mm2 and kN/mm2 for the same quantity (0.165 kN/mm2 would be 165 MPa yield for a plaster-filled polypropylene foam, which is physically impossible; red brick at 0.610 kN/mm2 = 610 MPa likewise). Load units for 'peak load' are never given. Because every strength value in the paper is either duplicated from another specimen or carries a unit that is off by orders of magnitude, no strength could be converted to MPa without inventing an interpretation, and none was.

The one internally consistent, unit-labelled figure is the measured density of the tested material, 1239.90 kg/m3 = 1.2399 g/cm3 (Table (c)); it is noted here only, since the specimen it belongs to is not a hollow-particle composite. No modulus, strain rate, test standard or test temperature is reported anywhere in the paper.
